data.content_ref: inline:The target's distinction between 'rational action' and 'inductive inference' fails because Popper's own criterion for preferring a theory (its survival of severe tests) implicitly relies on the assumption that the future will resemble the past. If corroboration reports only past performance without any inductive link to future success, then acting on it is methodologically arbitrary, not rational. To claim it is 'rational action' requires an expectation that past success indicates future reliability, which smuggles in the very principle of induction (uniformity of nature) that Popper explicitly rejected.
